A firewall filters network traffic. Blocks DDoS floods and slows password guessing. Phishing walks past it.
Catches phishing and the mail that carries ransomware.
Patching installs updates that fix known holes. A patched machine stops worms cold.
Restoring from backup makes ransomware worthless.
Multi-factor authentication asks for a second proof, like a code. Stops password guessing and stolen passwords.
An intrusion detection system watches for attacks and raises alarms. Cheap and weak against everything. Good to fill gaps.

This is a game about how attackers and defenders think. Everything is simulated: nothing touches a real device or network, and the app needs no internet.\n\nYou will type terminal commands, spot phishing, break old ciphers and defend a network.

• Terminal missions: story missions in a fake Linux terminal, plus puzzles.
• SOC analyst: sort emails and alerts into legit, phishing or escalate.
• Cipher Quest: break codes from Caesar to a toy Enigma.
• Tower defense: place defenses on a network map against waves of attacks.

Tap the ? button inside each one to see how to play.

Solving things earns points and skill XP (Linux, Crypto, Web, Network, Defense, Social engineering). Hints cost a few points but never block you.\n\nSolve something every day to grow your streak. The Codex unlocks short lessons as you go.

New to the command line? Start with the first Terminal mission: it teaches the basics step by step.\n\nNot sure what a word means? Open the Glossary from the Codex tab or from Settings. You can see this intro again in Settings.

Missions are story levels in a simulated Linux terminal. Read the brief, type commands (tap a chip to insert one, long-press a chip to see how it works) and find the hidden flag, then type submit flag{...}.

Objectives show your progress. The Trace meter rises when you do noisy things such as scan; at 100 percent you are caught and restart. Hints cost a few points but never block you.

Puzzles are standalone CTF challenges with helper tools (Base64, hex, hashes). Find the flag and type it in the Flag box.

A SOC (Security Operations Center) is the team that watches a company's emails, alerts and logs. Each shift is a queue of items. For each one choose:
• Legit: normal and safe.
• Phishing: a trick to steal passwords or money.
• Escalate: a real attack that a senior analyst must handle.

After each item you see the right answer and the clues to look for. Score at least 70 percent to pass. The daily shift is the same for everyone today. Story shifts unlock one after another, and some need a Terminal mission first.

Each level gives you a ciphertext (a scrambled message). Use the tools to decode it, then type the plaintext (the readable message) and press Check. Spaces, capitals and punctuation do not matter.\n\nChapters unlock in order and each brings new tools: frequency analysis, Caesar shift, Vigenère, Enigma and RSA. Hints cost a few points but never block you.

Protect the Database from waves of attacks that come in from the Internet. Before each wave, tap a node to build defenses. Each defense stops certain attacks, so read what it stops.

Budget is the money you can spend. Integrity is how many attacks can reach the Database before the network falls. Letters on the map are attacks: the legend explains them. Cleared waves give you more budget, and selling a defense returns half its cost.

The line “Next wave” tells you what is coming.

Your goal: find the flag, a secret text that looks like flag{some_words}, and hand it in with submit flag{...}.

• Trace (top): how suspicious you look to the defenders. Noisy commands such as scan raise it. At 100 percent you are caught and restart. Tap the ? next to it for more.
• Objectives: a checklist of what to do.
• Hints: cost a few points but never block you.
• The chips under the screen insert commands; long-press one to see how it works. Type help to list every command.

Concepts are explained in the Codex and in the Glossary.

A cipher scrambles a message. The scrambled text is the ciphertext; your goal is the plaintext, the readable message.

Use the tools below the ciphertext (one is already selected) to decode it, type the plaintext in the answer box and press Check. Spaces, capitals and punctuation do not matter.

In the Caesar tool a negative shift moves letters back, which is how you decrypt.

SOC stands for Security Operations Center: the team that watches a company's emails, alerts and logs.

Each shift is a queue. For every item decide:
• Legit: normal and safe.
• Phishing: a trick to steal passwords or money.
• Escalate: a real attack in progress; pass it to a senior analyst.

After each answer you see the right one and the clues to look for. Score at least 70 percent to pass.

Protect the Database (the red circle) from attacks that enter from the Internet.
• Budget is your money to build defenses.
• Integrity is how many attacks can reach the Database before you lose.
• Letters on the map are attacks: P phishing, W worm, R ransomware, D DDoS, B password guessing. The legend below the map explains each one.

Tap a node, such as the Router, to build a defense. The best choice depends on the next wave, shown under the map.
Counts how often each letter appears. In English E is the most common letter, so the most frequent letter often stands for E.
Moves every letter a fixed number of places along the alphabet. Change the shift until the output reads as words.
Like a Caesar shift, but a keyword changes the shift for every letter. Enter the key to decrypt.
Estimates how long the Vigenère key is. The true length scores clearly higher.
A toy Enigma machine. The same rotor positions encrypt and decrypt.
Public-key encryption. Enter n and e: the tool factors n, works out the private key and decrypts.
A negative shift moves letters back: that is how you decrypt.
Legit: normal and safe. Phishing: a trick to steal passwords or money. Escalate: a real attack that a senior analyst must handle.
Budget is the money you can spend on defenses. Integrity is how many attacks can reach the Database before the network falls. Letters on the map are attacks: see the legend below.
Try it: tap the Router (or any node in the list below) and build a defense that stops what is coming.
a flood of fake traffic (distributed denial of service)

Points come from solving things, minus the hints you used. Day streak counts the days in a row you solved something. Completed counts every mission, puzzle, SOC shift, cipher level and defense map you finished.
The team that watches a company\'s alerts, emails and logs around the clock and decides what is harmless and what is an attack.
A fake email or message that pretends to be someone you trust, to steal passwords or money. Look for lookalike addresses, urgency and odd links.
Hand a suspicious case to a senior analyst because it may be a real attack and needs a closer look.
A secret text, like flag{some_words}, hidden in a mission or puzzle. Finding it proves you solved the challenge. Hand it in with submit flag{...}.
How suspicious you look to the defenders. Noisy actions such as scanning raise it. At 100 percent you are caught and the mission restarts.
A text window where you type commands to talk to a computer. The terminal missions use a safe, simulated one.
Looking around before acting: which machines and services exist? Attackers and defenders both start here.
A fixed-length fingerprint of some data. The same input always gives the same hash, and you cannot turn a hash back into the original.
A method for scrambling a message so that only someone with the right key can read it.
The scrambled message you start with.
The readable message you get after decrypting. Type it in the answer box; spaces and punctuation do not matter.
Replace every letter with the one a fixed number of places along the alphabet. A shift of 3 turns A into D. To undo it, shift back by the same number (a negative shift).
Counting how often each letter appears. In English E is the most common, so the most frequent ciphertext letter often stands for E.
Trying many passwords or keys until one works. Limits, multi-factor login and long keys slow it down.
Logging in with a second proof besides the password, such as a code from your phone. A stolen password alone is no longer enough.
A flood of fake traffic from many machines that overloads a service so real users cannot reach it.
Malware that locks your files and demands money to unlock them. Good backups make it much less harmful.
Malware that spreads from machine to machine by itself, usually through unpatched software.
A filter that allows or blocks network traffic according to rules.
A watcher that looks at network traffic or logs and raises an alarm when something looks like an attack.
Installing the vendor\'s updates that fix known security holes.
A separate copy of your data. If files are lost or locked, you can restore them.
The money you can spend on defenses in Tower defense. It grows after each wave.
Your lives in Tower defense. Each attack that gets through to the Database lowers it. At zero the network falls.
Stories that link several games: finish steps in order.
